title: Digital Data Transmission
description: Turn signals into bits with PCM, share links with TDM, choose line codes and digital modulations, and check rates against Nyquist, Shannon and the bit error rate.

study.title: Explore: bits, symbols and channel capacity
study.body: A symbol with $M$ possible states (levels, phases, …) carries $\log_2 M$ bits, so the bit rate is $R_b = R_s\log_2 M$; the symbol rate $R_s$ is the **baud rate**. Hartley/Nyquist: a noiseless channel of bandwidth $B$ carries at most $2B$ symbols per second. Shannon gives the hard limit for a noisy channel; use $S/N$ as a power **ratio** (30 dB = 1000), never in dB. Drag the S/N: at high S/N every extra 3 dB buys about 1 bps/Hz.

study.title: Explore: PCM, companding and TDM
study.body: PCM samples at $f_s > 2f_{max}$ (telephony: 8 kHz), quantises each sample to one of $2^n$ levels and sends the $n$-bit code; each extra bit adds about 6 dB of signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio. **Companding** boosts small signals before a uniform quantiser (drag $\mu$; μ-law with μ = 255 in North America and Japan, A-law with A = 87.6 in Europe), so 8 bits give speech the quality of 12–13 linear bits. **TDM** sends the words of several channels in turn, one 125 µs frame per sample period: E1 = 32 slots × 8 bits × 8000 = 2.048 Mbps; T1 = (24 × 8 + 1) × 8000 = 1.544 Mbps.

study.title: Explore: line codes
study.body: **NRZ** holds the level for the whole bit: the fastest pattern (1010…) has a fundamental of only $R_b/2$, but long runs of equal bits give no transitions for clock recovery and unipolar NRZ has a DC component. **RZ** returns to zero halfway through each 1. **Manchester** (biphase) has a transition in the middle of every bit, here 1 = high→low and 0 = low→high as in Frenzel (Ethernet uses the opposite): easy clock recovery and no DC, at twice the bandwidth. Drag to send another byte.

study.title: Explore: digital modulation
study.body: Digital modulation keys the carrier's amplitude (**ASK**, on-off keying **OOK**), frequency (**FSK**) or phase (**PSK**); **QAM** varies amplitude and phase together. Each point in the I/Q **constellation** is one symbol of $\log_2 M$ bits: BPSK 1, QPSK 2, 8-PSK 3, 16-QAM 4, 64-QAM 6. Denser constellations put the points closer together, so they need more S/N for the same bit error rate: for BER = $10^{-6}$ roughly 11 dB C/N for BPSK but 20 dB for 16-QAM. Drag the bits per symbol.

study.title: Explore: bandwidth and spectral efficiency
study.body: Nyquist: $R_s$ symbols per second need at least $R_s/2$ of baseband bandwidth, or $R_s$ around a carrier (two sidebands). Practical **raised-cosine** filters with roll-off $\alpha$ (0 to 1) need $(1 + \alpha)$ times that, but cause no intersymbol interference. Spectral efficiency $R_b/B$ (bps/Hz) grows with $\log_2 M$. To compare modulations independent of bandwidth, use $E_b/N_0$, the energy per bit over the noise density. Drag $\alpha$.

study.title: Spread spectrum and OFDM
study.body: **Spread spectrum** deliberately uses far more bandwidth than the data need. **FHSS** hops the carrier over many channels in a pseudorandom order; **DSSS** multiplies each bit by a fast pseudorandom chip sequence. Despreading with the same code collapses the wanted signal back to the data bandwidth while spreading interference out: the **processing gain** is the chip rate over the bit rate, and users with different codes can share one band (CDMA). **OFDM** splits a fast stream over many slow, orthogonal subcarriers spaced $1/T_u$ apart (the useful symbol time), which makes it robust against multipath (Wi-Fi, LTE, DAB).

study.title: Error detection and correction
study.body: A **parity** bit makes the number of 1s even (or odd), which detects any single-bit error. A **checksum** adds up the bytes of a block; a **CRC** divides the block by a generator polynomial and sends the remainder, which catches practically all burst errors. **Forward error correction** (FEC) adds enough redundancy for the receiver to correct errors itself, without a retransmission. A Hamming code with $p$ check bits corrects one error in $m$ data bits when $2^p \geq m + p + 1$; the code rate is $m/(m + p)$.

steps.title: Bits and bauds
steps.body: Parallel transmission sends all bits of a word at once on separate wires: fast, but only over short distances. Longer links send the data **serially**, one symbol after another. The **baud rate** $R_s$ counts symbols per second. A symbol with $M$ distinct states (voltage levels, phases, …) carries $\log_2 M$ bits.

steps.prompt: A modem sends {{Rs|baud}} with {{M}} different symbols. What is its bit rate?
steps.explanation: {{M}} symbols carry $\log_2$ {{M}} = {{b}} bits each, so $R_b = R_s\log_2 M$ = {{Rs|baud}} × {{b}} = **{{Rs*b|bps}}**. Bit rate equals baud rate only for binary (2-state) symbols.

steps.title: How fast can a channel go?
steps.body: Without noise, a channel of bandwidth $B$ carries at most $2B$ symbols per second (Hartley/Nyquist), so more levels mean more bits. Noise sets a hard limit, found by Shannon. In his formula $S/N$ is a power **ratio**: convert from dB first with $10^{dB/10}$.

steps.prompt: A channel has a bandwidth of {{B|Hz}} and a signal-to-noise ratio of {{snr}} dB. What is its Shannon capacity?

steps.title: Pulse-code modulation
steps.body: PCM turns an analog signal into bits in three steps: **sample** it (faster than twice the highest frequency), **quantise** each sample to one of $2^n$ levels and **encode** the level as an $n$-bit word. The words of all channels are then sent serially.

steps.prompt: A PCM recorder samples {{ch}} channel(s) at {{fs|Hz}} with {{n}}-bit samples. What is the bit rate?
Put the stages of a PCM transmitter in order.
steps.explanation: The filter removes everything above $f_s/2$ **before** sampling, the S/H freezes the value, the ADC quantises and encodes it, and a shift register sends the bits serially (usually interleaved with other channels in a TDM frame).

steps.title: Line codes
steps.body: Before the bits go onto a cable they are given a shape. Shown for the byte 10110010: **NRZ** holds the level for the whole bit; **RZ** returns to zero halfway through each 1; **Manchester** always switches in the middle of the bit (1 = high→low, 0 = low→high), so the receiver can recover the clock from any data.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows the byte {{P|bin|8}} in Manchester code (1 = high→low, 0 = low→high in the middle of the bit)?
steps.explanation: Manchester has a transition in the **middle of every bit**: a 1 starts high and drops, a 0 starts low and rises. The graph with only bit-boundary changes is NRZ, the one with short pulses for the 1s only is RZ.

steps.prompt: At the same bit rate, Manchester code needs about twice the bandwidth of NRZ.
steps.explanation: True. The fastest NRZ pattern 1010… makes one cycle per **two** bits ($f = R_b/2$); Manchester can change level every half bit, so its fastest pattern makes one cycle per bit ($f = R_b$). The price buys clock recovery and zero DC.

steps.prompt: A signal with frequencies up to {{fm|Hz}} is digitized with PCM at {{k}} times the Nyquist rate, using {{n}}-bit samples.

ask.prompt: What is the bit rate?
ask.explanation: Nyquist rate = $2f_{max}$ = {{2*fm|Hz}}, so $f_s$ = {{k}} × {{2*fm|Hz}} = {{fs|Hz}}. $R_b = f_s n$ = {{fs|Hz}} × {{n}} = **{{fs*n|bps}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio for a full-scale sine?
ask.explanation: $\text{SNR}_q \approx 6.02n + 1.76$ = 6.02 × {{n}} + 1.76 = **{{6.02*n+1.76||4}} dB**. The sample rate does not matter here (oversampling with filtering would add a little).

steps.prompt: A PCM system must reach a signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio of at least {{S}} dB for a full-scale sine ($\text{SNR}_q = 6.02n + 1.76$ dB). How many bits per sample are needed?
A TDM system carries {{N}} PCM voice channels (8 kHz sampling, 8 bits per sample). Each frame also contains {{F}} framing/signalling bit(s).

ask.prompt: How many bits does one frame contain?
ask.explanation: Each channel contributes one 8-bit sample per frame: {{N}} × 8 + {{F}} = **{{8*N+F||5}} bits**.

ask.prompt: What is the line bit rate?
ask.explanation: One frame per sample period (125 µs): $R$ = {{8*N+F||5}} bits × 8000 frames/s = **{{(8*N+F)*8000|bps|4}}**.

ask.prompt: How long does one bit last on the line?

steps.prompt: A European E1 frame has 32 time slots of 8 bits (30 voice channels, slot 0 for framing, slot 16 for signalling) and is repeated 8000 times per second. What is the E1 line rate?
steps.explanation: 32 × 8 = 256 bits per frame, × 8000 frames/s = **2.048 Mbps**. 1.92 Mbps counts only the 30 voice slots; 1.544 Mbps is the North-American T1 ((24 × 8 + 1) × 8000); 256 kbps forgets the 8000 frames per second.

steps.prompt: A noiseless channel has a bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: What is its maximum bit rate with {{M}}-level symbols (Hartley)?
How many levels $M$ are needed at least to carry {{2*B*x|bps}}, if $M$ must be a power of two?
ask.explanation: $\log_2 M \geq \frac{C}{2B}$ = {{2*B*x|bps}} / {{2*B|Hz}} = {{x}} bits per symbol → round up to {{ceil(x)}} bits: $M = 2^{ {{ceil(x)}} }$ = **{{2^ceil(x)}}**.

steps.prompt: A channel has a bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: What is its Shannon capacity at $S/N$ = {{snr}} dB?
What $S/N$ (in dB) is needed at least to carry {{eff*B|bps}}?
ask.explanation: $C/B$ = {{eff}} bps/Hz, so $1 + S/N = 2^{ {{eff}} }$ → $S/N$ = {{2^eff-1}} = **{{10*log10(2^eff-1)||3}} dB**. Real modems need several dB more than this limit.

steps.prompt: Data at {{Rb|bps}} is sent as a baseband line code. The fastest pattern sets the fundamental frequency the cable must pass.

ask.prompt: What is that fundamental frequency for NRZ?
ask.explanation: The pattern 1010… gives one period per two bits: $f = R_b/2$ = **{{Rb/2|Hz}}** (Hartley: $C = 2B$). For clean edges allow several times more.

ask.prompt: What is that fundamental frequency for Manchester code?
ask.explanation: Manchester can change level every half bit, so its fastest pattern (a run of equal bits) has one period per bit: $f = R_b$ = **{{Rb|Hz}}**, twice NRZ.

steps.prompt:
A μ-law compressor ($\mu$ = 255, $V_{max}$ = {{Vm|V}}) gets an input of {{vin|V}}. Use the μ-law with $x = v_{in}/V_{max}$:
$$v_{out} = V_{max}\frac{\ln(1 + \mu x)}{\ln(1 + \mu)}$$

ask.prompt: What is the output voltage?
What is the gain of the compressor at this level, in dB?
ask.explanation: $v_{out}$ = {{vo|V}}, so $A$ = {{vo|V}} / {{vin|V}} = {{vo/vin||3}} = **{{20*log10(vo/vin)||3}} dB**. Small inputs get much more gain than large ones; the expander at the receiver undoes this.

steps.prompt: The byte {{P|bin|8}} is sent with the line code below. Which code is it?
steps.explanation: NRZ only changes at bit boundaries and holds the level for a whole bit. RZ sends a half-bit pulse for each 1 and returns to zero. Manchester has a transition in the middle of **every** bit, whatever the data.

steps.prompt: A 3 kHz channel with $S/N$ = 30 dB can carry at most $3000\log_2(1 + 30)$ ≈ 14.9 kbps.
steps.explanation: False: 30 dB must first be converted to a power ratio, $10^{30/10}$ = 1000. Then $C$ = 3000 × $\log_2$(1001) = 3000 × 9.97 ≈ **29.9 kbps**.

steps.title: Constellations
steps.body: Plot each symbol as a point: the distance from the origin is the carrier amplitude, the angle its phase (I and Q are the in-phase and quadrature components). $M$ points carry $\log_2 M$ bits per symbol. Drag through BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK and 16-QAM.

steps.prompt: Match each modulation to its number of bits per symbol.
steps.explanation: Bits per symbol = $\log_2 M$: 2, 4, 8, 16 and 64 points give 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 bits. At the same symbol rate (and bandwidth) 64-QAM therefore carries 6× the data of BPSK, but it needs a far better S/N.

steps.prompt: The constellation of a modulator running at {{Rs|baud}} is shown below.

ask.prompt: How many bits does each symbol carry?
ask.explanation: Count the points: $M$ = {{2^b}}. Bits per symbol = $\log_2$ {{2^b}} = **{{b}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the bit rate?
ask.explanation: $M$ = {{2^b}} points → {{b}} bits per symbol. $R_b = R_s\log_2 M$ = {{Rs|baud}} × {{b}} = **{{b*Rs|bps}}**.

steps.prompt: A {{Rb|bps}} stream is sent with {{2^b}}-QAM and raised-cosine filtering with roll-off $\alpha$ = {{a}}.

ask.prompt: What is the symbol rate?
ask.explanation: {{2^b}}-QAM carries {{b}} bits per symbol: $R_s = R_b/\log_2 M$ = {{Rb|bps}} / {{b}} = **{{Rs|baud}}**.

ask.prompt: What RF bandwidth does the signal occupy?
ask.explanation: $R_s$ = {{Rs|baud}}. Passband: $B = (1 + \alpha)R_s$ = {{1+a}} × {{Rs|baud}} = **{{(1+a)*Rs|Hz}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the spectral efficiency?

steps.prompt: A link carries {{Rb|bps}} in a noise bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}. Use $S/N = (E_b/N_0)(R_b/B)$.

ask.prompt: The measured $C/N$ is {{cn}} dB. What is $E_b/N_0$ in dB?
The modulation needs $E_b/N_0$ = {{eb}} dB. What $C/N$ is needed?
ask.explanation: $R_b/B$ = {{eff}} → {{10*log10(eff)||3}} dB. $C/N = E_b/N_0 + 10\log_{10}(R_b/B)$ = {{eb}} + {{10*log10(eff)||3}} = **{{eb+10*log10(eff)||3}} dB**. Packing more bits per hertz costs C/N.

steps.prompt: A DSSS system spreads {{Rb|bps}} of data with a chip rate of {{Rc|chip/s|5}}. In the spread bandwidth the signal arrives {{j}} dB **below** the noise.

ask.prompt: What is the processing gain in dB?
What is the S/N after despreading?
ask.explanation: $G_p$ = $10\log_{10}$({{Rc/Rb||4}}) = {{G||3}} dB. Despreading lifts the S/N by the processing gain: −{{j}} + {{G||3}} = **{{G-j||3}} dB**. That is how a signal hidden below the noise can be received.

steps.prompt: Data words of {{m}} bits are protected with a single-error-correcting Hamming code.

ask.prompt: How many check bits $p$ are needed?
What is the code rate (data bits / transmitted bits)?
ask.explanation: With $p$ = {{p}} check bits ($2^{ {{p}} }$ = {{2^p||4}} ≥ {{m+p+1}}), each codeword has {{m+p}} bits: rate = {{m}}/{{m+p}} = **{{m/(m+p)||3}}**. Longer words need relatively fewer check bits.

steps.prompt: A {{Rb|bps}} link has a bit error rate of $10^{-{{nb}}}$.

ask.prompt: How many bit errors occur on average in {{T}} s?
ask.explanation: Bits sent = {{Rb|bps}} × {{T}} s = {{Rb*T|bit}}. Errors = BER × bits = $10^{-{{nb}}}$ × {{Rb*T|bit}} = **{{Rb*ber*T||3}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the average time between two bit errors?
ask.explanation: Errors per second = {{Rb|bps}} × $10^{-{{nb}}}$ = {{Rb*ber||3}}, so on average one error every 1 / {{Rb*ber||3}} = **{{1/(Rb*ber)|s}}**.

steps.prompt: With **even** parity, which parity bit is appended to the 7-bit ASCII code {{c|bin|7}}?
steps.explanation: {{c|bin|7}} contains {{ones}} ones. Even parity makes the total number of 1s even, so the parity bit is **{{mod(ones, 2)}}** (total {{ones+mod(ones,2)}} ones). The receiver flags an error when it counts an odd number.

steps.prompt: A single parity bit detects any error in which two bits of the word are flipped.
steps.explanation: False. Flipping two bits changes the number of 1s by 0 or ±2, so the parity stays correct and the error passes unnoticed. Parity only detects an **odd** number of bit errors; CRCs and Hamming codes do better.

steps.prompt: A radio link carries {{N}} telephone channels (PCM: 8 kHz × 8 bits each, ignore framing overhead) with {{2^b}}-QAM and raised-cosine roll-off $\alpha$ = {{a}}.

ask.prompt: What is the symbol rate?
What RF bandwidth does the link occupy?

steps.prompt: A designer wants to send {{eta*B|bps}} through a {{B|Hz}} channel. Use Shannon's limit.

ask.prompt: What is the minimum $S/N$ in dB?
What is the corresponding minimum $E_b/N_0$ in dB?
ask.explanation: $S/N$ = {{2^eta-1}}. $E_b/N_0 = (S/N)(B/R_b)$ = {{2^eta-1}} / {{eta}} = {{(2^eta-1)/eta||3}} = **{{10*log10((2^eta-1)/eta)||3}} dB**. Even at very low rates it never drops below −1.6 dB, the ultimate Shannon limit.

steps.prompt: A {{Rb|bps}} stream must fit into a {{B|Hz}} radio channel with raised-cosine roll-off $\alpha$ = {{a}}.

ask.prompt: How many bits per symbol are needed at least?
ask.explanation: Maximum symbol rate: $R_s = B/(1 + \alpha)$ = {{B|Hz}} / {{1+a}} = {{B/(1+a)|baud}}. Bits per symbol ≥ {{Rb|bps}} / {{B/(1+a)|baud}} = {{x||3}} → **{{n}}** (round up).

ask.prompt: How many points does the constellation then have?
ask.explanation: Needed: $R_b(1 + \alpha)/B$ = {{x||3}} bits per symbol → {{n}} bits → $M = 2^{ {{n}} }$ = **{{2^n}}** points.

steps.prompt: A receiver with a noise figure of {{NF}} dB receives {{Pr}} dBm of a {{Rb|bps}} BPSK signal. The noise density is $N_0$ = −174 dBm/Hz + NF; $E_b = P_r/R_b$.

ask.prompt: What is $E_b/N_0$ in dB?
BPSK needs $E_b/N_0$ = 10.5 dB for a BER of $10^{-6}$. What is the margin (negative if the link fails)?

steps.prompt: An OFDM system sends {{Nsc}} data subcarriers in parallel, each with {{2^b}}-QAM. One OFDM symbol, including the guard interval, lasts {{Ts|s}}; the FEC code rate is {{cr}}.

ask.prompt: What is the raw bit rate (before FEC)?
ask.explanation: Per OFDM symbol: {{Nsc}} subcarriers × {{b}} bits = {{Nsc*b}} bits. $R$ = {{Nsc*b}} / {{Ts|s}} = **{{Nsc*b/Ts|bps}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the user data rate after FEC?
ask.explanation: Raw: {{Nsc}} × {{b}} / {{Ts|s}} = {{Nsc*b/Ts|bps}}. Only the fraction {{cr}} is data: **{{Nsc*b/Ts*cr|bps}}**. (48 subcarriers, 64-QAM, 4 µs and rate 3/4 is the 54 Mbps mode of Wi-Fi 802.11a/g.)

steps.prompt: A satellite navigation signal carries {{Rb}} bps of data spread with a chip rate of {{Rc|chip/s|4}}. At the antenna it is {{j}} dB below the thermal noise in the spread bandwidth.

ask.prompt: What is the processing gain in dB?
What is the S/N of the data after despreading?
ask.explanation: $G_p$ = 10 log({{Rc/Rb||4}}) = {{G||3}} dB. S/N = −{{j}} + {{G||3}} = **{{G-j||3}} dB**: plenty, thanks to the very low data rate.

steps.prompt: Words of {{m}} data bits get the minimum number of Hamming check bits for single-error correction and are sent at a line rate of {{R|bps|4}}. What is the useful data rate?
A {{Rs|baud}} QPSK signal must fit into a {{B|Hz}} channel. Set the **largest** raised-cosine roll-off that still fits (gentler filters are cheaper).
steps.explanation: Passband: $B = (1 + \alpha)R_s$ → $\alpha = B/R_s - 1$ = {{B|Hz}} / {{Rs|baud}} − 1 = **{{ratio-1}}**. Then the spectrum ends exactly at the channel edges ±{{B/2|Hz}}.
